rv.q: Jamie Lloyd’s Tom Hiddleston and Hayley Atwell-starring take on ‘Much Ado’ is a ridiculous, ecstatic, hilarious masterpiece...
From start to finish, the show is a joy: a love song to the exhilaration, pain and giddy nonsense of passion, with Tom Hiddleston and Hayley Atwell absolutely acing it at the helm.

The boldest stroke (design: Soutra Gilmour) is a sustained shower of pink confetti. It’s faintly magical to behold; on another level, it chimes with the play’s tragicomic mix of autumnal wistfulness and amorous adventure.
This is a thoroughly weird and absolutely wonderful re-conceptualisation, turning Shakespeare’s comedy, which narrowly swerves tragedy, into an old school house party cum modern romcom.

The simplicity of the staging and the licensed showboating of the stars gives an idea of what theatre in Shakespeare's day might have been like, only with more Jagerbombs, airhorn blasts and disco lights.
It’s a total hoot with a tender heart.
Here is a buoyant lesson in how to put on popular Shakespeare: clear, noisy, direct and infectious.
The plaudits for this show will continue to echo long after its too-short run has concluded.
Lloyd’s mischievous club-culture reinvention of Much Ado About Nothing has colour, passion and, in the form of Tom Hiddleston, a head-miked leading man who is absolutely in command.
The chemistry between them is like a kilo of sodium dumped in the village pond: fizzy, flashing and explosive.
Fluffy though his staging might look, Lloyd strips the frills from this story to reveal the push and pull of rejection and reconciliation at its heart.
Tom Hiddleston is a wonderfully wry Benedick
Hugely camp, incredibly romantic and wildly fun.
Long-time friends Hiddleston and Atwell turn these ingredients into a full-on banquet of both blissful comedy and ecstatic romance.
The production is big, broad and for all its contemporary trimmings, absolutely Shakespearean in the way that it welcomes everyone into the entertainment.
It would take a constitution of steel – not to say hotpants of lead – to stay immune to the technicolour joie de vivre.
An exciting version of Shakespeare that must be seen.
Thankfully the team have created such a wholeheartedly joyous production, that it will assuredly lay the ghost of the recent disappointing Tempest to rest.
This sets a fast pace with the playing loud and lively.
This is an earnest attempt to bring Shakespeare down to the level of cruise-ship entertainment.
Overall, I defy anyone, from the harshest Shakespearean traditionalist, to the die-hard Loki stan, not to enjoy this sparkling rendition of Shakespeare meets Mamma Mia.
This show is camp, mischievous, exuberant, romantic, life, love and laughter-affirming bliss.
Jamie Lloyd’s Much Ado About Nothing is a daring and inventive production that showcases Shakespeare through a modern lens.
So a mixed evening - there's definitely a fun premise here, and in stark contrast to Elektra a sense of embracing a new audience without either patronising them or talking over their heads.

cn.t: Lloyd's disco-infused, confetti-drenched production wins widespread acclaim as joyful and irresistible, with Hiddleston and Atwell's chemistry sparking delight, though one critic finds the concept overwhelms Shakespeare's text.

vr.q: Jamie Lloyd has directed maybe my favorite version of it ever
